body_paragraphs: Thursday looked like relief after Wednesday's damage - the S&P jumped 1.7% to 7,437.64 and the Nasdaq 2.8% to 25,122.18, Microsoft alone up 15% on AI earnings that finally showed a payoff. But the bond market didn't join the party: the 10-year rose another 8 basis points to 4.704%, its highest close of the run, even as stocks celebrated. That's the second day in a row rates have refused to confirm what equities are telling you, with tomorrow's jobs report the next real test.

Iran's war took a similarly ambiguous turn. Tehran's army claims it struck US assets at bases in Kuwait and Bahrain overnight - neither government has confirmed it - and the US, notably, launched no fresh strikes for the first time since Wednesday's heavy wave. Read generously, that's a pause. Egypt, meanwhile, got its first taste of the conflict when a drone of unknown origin hit two gas vessels at its Damietta port. Oil eased anyway, down to $87.78, on early signs Hormuz shipping is recovering - a market betting on calm it can't yet verify.

Miami's stakes are smaller but real: the Marlins lost at the Mets to snap a three-game streak, and the trade-deadline noise around Otto Lopez got louder, with Boston reportedly eyeing a bigger package that includes catcher Liam Hicks. Three days to the deadline. And if you want something that isn't waiting on tomorrow's data, tonight's rabbit hole revisits Sartre's case that freedom and responsibility are inseparable - worth sitting with on a day when a Fed vote, a war room, and an unconfirmed Iranian claim all made decisions that landed on you anyway.

themes.title: New research says your brain decides earlier than the textbook model claims
themes.thesis: The tidy picture of decisions rising cleanly from sensation to judgment turns out to be wrong - even basic sensory regions are already shaping the verdict.
themes.synthesis: A study led by University of Illinois engineering professor Yurii Vlasov, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found decision-related signals in the primary somatosensory cortex - a region traditionally thought to handle only basic sensory processing. Rather than information flowing strictly upward from sensation to the prefrontal cortex where a 'choice' gets made, the research shows rapid feedback loops in which higher brain regions shape even early sensory processing. The findings are drawing interest from AI researchers looking to design systems that think more like biological brains while using far less power.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the Vlasov PNAS findings in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: It's a small, well-evidenced correction to a very confident old model of how choices get made - a useful thing to sit with on a day when a Fed vote and an unconfirmed military claim both reminded Alex how much of what shapes a decision happens before anyone notices they're deciding.

themes.title: A supervolcano that erupted 7,300 years ago is quietly refilling
themes.thesis: Deep time is still running underneath Japan, on a schedule that makes today's news cycle look like a rounding error.
themes.synthesis: Researchers at Kobe University used seismic surveys to detect a magma reservoir refilling beneath Japan's Kikai Caldera, the site of the largest Holocene-era eruption roughly 7,300 years ago. The reservoir sits unusually close to the surface, 2.5 to 6 kilometers down, and chemical analysis suggests the magma is newly injected rather than leftover material from the ancient eruption. The study doesn't suggest an eruption is imminent, but it offers a rare direct look at how giant caldera systems - including ones like Yellowstone - actually recharge over millennia.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the Kobe University findings in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: It's a genuine piece of appreciation-worthy science with no urgency attached to it at all - a useful counterweight on a day otherwise built entirely around things that feel urgent right now.

beautiful_thing.title: The cloud paintings of Baruj Salinas
beautiful_thing.creator: Baruj Salinas
beautiful_thing.body: Salinas, a Havana-born architect turned painter exiled from Cuba in 1959, spent the late 1970s in Barcelona working alongside Joan Miró and Antoni Tàpies, where he began a sustained series of abstract works built around clouds - a subject he returned to for decades, alongside a lifelong interest in cosmology. He co-founded the Grupo de Artistas Latinoamericanos in 1960s Miami and eventually settled back in Coral Gables, where he taught at Miami Dade College until his death in 2024. His work is held in the collections of the Art Institute of Chicago and the National Institute of Fine Arts in Mexico City.

daily_puzzle.prompt: A runner improves her mile time by 10% on Monday, then improves that new time by another 10% on Tuesday. After both improvements, she's running a 6-minute-45-second mile. What was her time before Monday's improvement?
daily_puzzle.hint: Two successive 10% cuts don't add up to a 20% cut - work out what they actually multiply the original time by, then undo that.
daily_puzzle.solution: 8 minutes 20 seconds. 6:45 is 405 seconds; two successive 10% reductions leave 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81 of the original time, so 405 / 0.81 = 500 seconds, or 8:20.
daily_puzzle.explanation: Percentage cuts compound multiplicatively, not additively - undoing them means dividing by the product of the factors, not adding the percentages back.

threads.title: 2026 CRE capital markets under pressure
threads.current_state: South Florida commercial sales volume remains down 13% year over year, and the summer's biggest single industrial deal - Waste Management's $379M purchase of 146 acres in Medley - was 96% seller-financed. Miami's average office asking rent, $59.66/sq ft, is now the highest of any US market, ahead of New York's $50.56. Two individual July deals put dollar figures behind that story: Pebb Capital's $69M-financed purchase of a Miami Beach office building, and a $24.5M Wynwood commercial sale.

timeline.summary: First tracked: CBRE Q2 update shows deal volume down 24% YoY, construction spending below plan, hiring slowing.
South Florida-specific data surfaces: commercial sales volume down 13% year over year to $5.42B in H1 2026.
Waste Management pays $379M for 146 acres in Medley to build a landfill; $366M of the price, 96%, is seller financing rather than a bank loan.

A LoopNet analysis of roughly 5,000 office listings finds Miami's average asking rent, $59.66/sq ft, now the highest in the US, ahead of New York's $50.56 - a sign of how much capital has relocated to Miami since 2020 even as deal volume overall stays soft.

Pebb Capital buys a Miami Beach office building with $69M in ACORE Capital financing; a Wynwood commercial parcel sells for $24.5M, the region's priciest trade that week - real transactions behind the aggregate rent data.

threads.title: Miami Marine Stadium's restoration referendum
threads.current_state: Miami voters decide Marine Stadium's future in an August 18 referendum (Referendum #172) on a 40-year management deal with Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and local partner Breakwater Hospitality. Under the deal, the city keeps 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with up to $10M toward restoration up front, followed by a separate $65-85M restoration bond. Early voting runs August 3-16; partial pile and seating repairs are already underway with county and state grant money.

timeline.summary: First tracked: City Commission approved the Global Spectrum/Oak View management deal in February; referendum set for August 18; partial restoration already underway.

Additional detail surfaces: the deal is formally Referendum #172, with early voting set for August 3-16 and a specified revenue split (93% events, 85% sponsorship) plus a separate $65-85M restoration bond beyond the initial $10M.
